message.content:
Read `docs/brief.md` in full first, then `CLAUDE.md`. The brief's table names, column names, endpoint paths, file paths and response shapes are a contract; hidden tests use them exactly.
Project state: Next 16.4.2 scaffold, Prisma 7.10.1 + @prisma/adapter-pg, @supabase/ssr, zod 4, vitest, shadcn v4, npm with package-lock. `supabase/config.toml` exists; `supabase/migrations/` is empty. No app code yet.
Decisions I have already made. Do not reopen them, but tell me if the brief contradicts one.

1. Priority order is the brief's: billing lib -> schema + RLS + storage -> auth helper + API (leases, payments, approve/reject/void, allocation) -> seed -> webhook + gateway bills -> collections report -> minimal UI -> REVIEW.md, DECISIONS.md, README, ai-logs. UI is last and skeletal if time is short.
2. `src/lib/billing.ts` is pure. Date math is done on (year, month, day) integers or `Date.UTC` only; never `new Date(string)` with local parsing, never local getters. Must pass the Aisyah worked example and the parseRinggitToSen vectors exactly.
3. One timezone helper module, `src/lib/myt.ts`: `todayInMalaysia(now: Date): string`, `parseMalaysiaLocal('YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm'): Date` (treat as +08:00), `formatMalaysia(date)`. Every "today" and every date<->instant conversion in the app goes through it. The collections report groups by `received_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kuala_Lumpur'` in SQL with `generate_series` so empty months appear.
4. Money: bigint sen in Postgres, `BigInt` in Prisma, `number` only at the JSON edge.
5. Prisma connects as the database owner, so RLS does not apply to it. Authorization for every route lives in one helper: `getCaller(req)` accepts `Authorization: Bearer <token>` or the session cookie, calls `supabase.auth.getUser()`, then loads role + org from `memberships` or `tenants.user_id` via Prisma. Never user_metadata. Rules: no valid login -> 401; record in another org or another tenant's record -> 404; visible record but role not allowed -> 403. IDs in bodies are checked against the caller's org.
6. RLS is the real wall for the Data API and Storage, exactly per the brief's matrix. Helper SQL functions `app.current_org_id()` and `app.current_tenant_id()` (SECURITY DEFINER, STABLE, reading memberships/tenants by `auth.uid()`), used in policies. `REVOKE ALL` from anon on everything. authenticated gets SELECT per matrix; tenants get `UPDATE (phone)` column grant on tenants with a policy `user_id = auth.uid()`. No INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE grants otherwise. audit_log: BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE trigger that raises, so even the owner cannot change it. Any function I create in `public` is `REVOKE EXECUTE FROM anon, authenticated` unless needed.
7. Storage: private bucket `payment-slips` created in a migration, policies on `storage.objects` for INSERT and SELECT restricted to staff/manager whose `app.current_org_id()::text = (storage.foldername(name))[1]`. Server issues short-lived signed URLs. Slip validation: JPEG/PNG/PDF, <= 5 MB; if the payment insert fails after upload, delete the object.
8. Concurrency: every payment mutation (record, approve, void, webhook settle) runs in one Prisma transaction that first does `SELECT id FROM leases WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE`, serialising per lease. Webhook also locks the `gateway_bills` row FOR UPDATE and `payments.gateway_bill_id` is UNIQUE. Lease overlap: `btree_gist` extension + `EXCLUDE USING gist (unit_id WITH =, daterange(start_date, end_date, '[]') WITH &&)` on leases, mapped to 409. Lease creation inserts lease + all invoices in one transaction.
9. Allocation: one function `allocate(tx, paymentId)` ordering invoices by due_date, then kind deposit before rent, then period_index; fills unpaid amounts; remainder to `payments.unapplied_sen`. Void deletes that payment's allocations only. Cap check: total invoices - total allocated - total pending_verification payments on the lease, computed inside the lock.
10. Gateway bill id: `bill_` + 32 hex chars from `crypto.randomBytes(16)`. Webhook: parse `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, build source from all fields except x_signature sorted by key, HMAC-SHA256 with `GATEWAY_X_SIGNATURE_KEY`, compare with `timingSafeEqual`; response codes exactly per the brief's table; never log the key or the payload.
11. Env names are the brief's: NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY, SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY, DATABASE_URL, DIRECT_URL, GATEWAY_X_SIGNATURE_KEY. `.env.example` committed with local values and a comment per variable. `.env.local` git-ignored.
12. Seed: `npm run seed` -> `scripts/seed.ts` with tsx. Creates auth users with the admin API (service key), one shared password `Rent2026!demo`, then orgs, memberships, units, tenants, and then creates leases and payments by calling the real service functions with the right actor (manager records cash -> approved; staff records bank transfer with an uploaded tiny PNG slip -> manager approves). Must be re-runnable only on a fresh `npx supabase db reset`.
13. `next.config.ts`: set `cacheComponents: false` and remove partialPrefetching. All dates rendered as Malaysia-time strings on the server to avoid hydration warnings.
14. Tests: vitest. Billing lib tests (worked example, anchors on Jan 31, leap year, short last period, parseRinggitToSen vectors, invoiceStatus boundary at 2026-03-01T16:00:00Z). An allocation unit test. These are cheap and the brief lists them as a bonus.

No code: A. The SQL for the first migration: all tables with the brief's names and columns plus what we need (created_at, status enums as CHECK constraints or Postgres enums, `payments.gateway_bill_id UNIQUE`, FKs with indexes, the exclusion constraint, the audit trigger). Then the RLS policy list as a table: table x role x operation x predicate. Then grants. Then the storage bucket and policies. B. File layout: `src/lib/billing.ts`, `src/lib/myt.ts`, `src/lib/auth/getCaller.ts`, `src/lib/db/prisma.ts`, `src/lib/supabase/{server,browser,admin}.ts`, `src/services/{leases,payments,allocation,gatewayBills,reports}.ts`, `src/lib/http.ts` (error -> status mapper, JSON helpers), route files per the brief's paths, `scripts/seed.ts`, `gateway-sim.mjs`. C. The slice order with a time estimate per slice that fits in 2h40m of building, leaving 30 min for REVIEW.md, DECISIONS.md, README and ai-logs. D. Anything in the brief that you think contradicts a decision above, or that I have missed.
Stop after the plan. I will review it before anything is written.

## 1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai .../artifact/... link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{...}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

# Project rules

Rent collection system for property managers. Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript), Supabase local (Postgres, Auth, RLS), Prisma 7 with pg adapter, shadcn/ui, Tailwind, Vitest, npm (graders run npm install / npm run seed / npm run build && npm start).

## Non-negotiables
- Money is integer sen (`*_sen` bigint); currency MYR. No float arithmetic on money. Rounding happens only in `src/lib/billing.ts` (pure, tested directly by the graders).

## 1. The Business

You are building part of the rent collection module of a property management platform used by Malaysian property management companies.

- Each organization (a property management company) rents units to tenants under leases.
- A lease produces invoices: an optional deposit, plus one rent invoice per monthly period.
- Tenants pay by cash, by bank transfer (with an uploaded slip), or online through a payment gateway. Payments are allocated to invoices.
- Business timezone: Asia/Kuala_Lumpur (UTC+8, no daylight saving). Currency: MYR (RM). 1 ringgit = 100 sen.
- Your server runs in UTC and our assessors work from several timezones. Every date and time the app shows or accepts is Malaysia time, whatever the timezone of the server or of the viewer's device.

### Roles

Role | Who | Can |
manager | Organization admin | Everything in their organization: create leases, record payments (approved immediately), approve, reject and void payments, read the audit log |
staff | Front desk | Read their organization's leases, invoices and payments; record payments (these wait for a manager's approval) |
tenant | Renter | Read their own profile, leases, invoices and payments; update their own phone number; pay online |

A staff member or manager belongs to exactly one organization. Nobody ever sees another organization's data.

## 2. Local Setup and Seed Data

Develop against a local Supabase stack (Docker and the Supabase CLI), not a cloud project. See Supabase local development. We grade by running your project on our machine from a fresh clone, with exactly these commands:

npx supabase db reset # rebuilds the database from supabase/migrations/
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local # we replace keys with the values from `npx supabase status` if they differ
npm run seed
npm run build && npm start

- Commit supabase/config.toml, supabase/migrations/, and an .env.example that lists every variable your app needs, with local values and a comment saying where each one comes from.
- npm run seed creates exactly the data below on a freshly reset database, through your normal code paths (your lease creation and payment logic), so the invoices and allocations it produces are the ones your app would produce.
- All seeded accounts share one password of your choice, which you submit with your work.

### Organizations and accounts

### Units and leases

### Payments on Aisyah's lease

- Bank transfer, RM 2,000.00, received 2026-03-01 00:30 Malaysia time, recorded by staff with a slip file, then approved by the manager.

## 3. Billing Rules - lib/billing.ts

Create lib/billing.ts (or src/lib/billing.ts). It must be pure: no I/O, no imports from Next.js, React, Supabase or Prisma, and no dependence on the timezone of the machine it runs on. Your app must use it, and we test it directly.
export type InvoiceKind = 'deposit' | 'rent'

export interface ScheduledInvoice {
kind: InvoiceKind
periodIndex: number | null // 0, 1, 2... for rent; null for the deposit
periodStart: string | null // 'YYYY-MM-DD'; null for the deposit
periodEnd: string | null // 'YYYY-MM-DD', inclusive; null for the deposit
dueDate: string // 'YYYY-MM-DD'
amountSen: number // integer
}

export function generateSchedule(lease: {
startDate: string // 'YYYY-MM-DD'
endDate: string // 'YYYY-MM-DD', inclusive (the tenant's last day)
monthlyRentSen: number
depositSen: number
}): ScheduledInvoice[]

export type InvoiceStatus = 'paid' | 'partially_paid' | 'unpaid' | 'overdue'

export function invoiceStatus(
invoice: { dueDate: string; amountSen: number; paidSen: number },
now: Date,
): InvoiceStatus

export function parseRinggitToSen(input: string): number

### generateSchedule

- Validation. Throw an Error if a date is not a real calendar date written as YYYY-MM-DD, if endDate is before startDate, if monthlyRentSen is not a positive integer, or if depositSen is not a non-negative integer.
- Deposit. If depositSen > 0, the first invoice is the deposit: kind: 'deposit', due on startDate, period fields null.
- Anchors. Rent periods are anchored on the start date. The anchor of period k is the start date plus k calendar months, always counted from the start date (never from the previous anchor). If that month has fewer days than the start day, use the month's last day. A lease starting on Jan 31 has anchors Jan 31, Feb 28 (Feb 29 in leap years), Mar 31, Apr 30, and so on.
- Periods. Period k runs from anchor k to the day before anchor k+1, and is due on anchor k. There is a period for every anchor on or before endDate.
- Last period. It is cut at endDate. If it is shorter than its full length, it costs monthlyRentSen x days used / days in the full period, rounded half up to the nearest sen. Every other period costs monthlyRentSen.
- Order. The deposit first, then rent by period index.
  Worked example (Aisyah's lease):
  Period | Kind | Dates | Due | Amount |
  | deposit | | 2026-01-31 | RM 3,000.00 |
  0 | rent | 2026-01-31 to 2026-02-27 | 2026-01-31 | RM 1,500.00 |
  1 | rent | 2026-02-28 to 2026-03-30 | 2026-02-28 | RM 1,500.00 |
  2 | rent | 2026-03-31 to 2026-04-29 | 2026-03-31 | RM 1,500.00 |
  3 | rent | 2026-04-30 to 2026-05-30 | 2026-04-30 | RM 1,500.00 |
  4 | rent | 2026-05-31 to 2026-06-29 | 2026-05-31 | RM 1,500.00 |
  5 | rent | 2026-06-30 to 2026-07-15 | 2026-06-30 | RM 774.19 |

Period 5 uses 16 of the 31 days from 2026-06-30 to 2026-07-30: 150000 x 16 / 31 = 77419.35, so 77419 sen.

### invoiceStatus

Apply these rules in order:

- paid if paidSen >= amountSen.
- overdue if today's Malaysia date is after dueDate. An invoice due 2026-03-01 becomes overdue at 2026-03-02 00:00 Malaysia time (2026-03-01T16:00:00Z), not a moment earlier.
- partially_paid if paidSen > 0.
- Otherwise unpaid.

### parseRinggitToSen

Turns what a user types into sen. It accepts digits with optional comma thousands separators (groups of exactly three digits) and an optional decimal part of one or two digits, ignoring whitespace around the value: "1,500.50" gives 150050, "1.15" gives 115, "7" gives 700. Anything else throws an Error, for example "", "-5", "1.234", "1e3", "RM 10", "1,23".

## 4. Payments

### Recording a payment

- Staff and managers record cash or bank transfer payments on a lease: the amount, the method, and the date and time the money was received (entered and shown in Malaysia time).
- A bank transfer needs a slip: a JPEG, PNG or PDF of at most 5 MB, stored in Supabase Storage (section 6). If recording fails after the upload, the file must not be left behind.
- A payment recorded by a manager is approved immediately. A payment recorded by staff is pending_verification until a manager approves or rejects it.
- Cap. A new payment may not be more than the lease's remaining balance (the total of all its invoices minus everything allocated to them) minus the total of the lease's payments still pending_verification. Paying future periods in advance is allowed within the cap.

### Approving, rejecting and voiding (managers only)

- Approve a pending_verification payment. At that moment, check again that it is not more than the lease's remaining balance. If it is, refuse and leave it pending.
- Reject a pending_verification payment, with a reason of at least 5 characters.
- Void an approved payment, with a reason of at least 5 characters. Voiding removes that payment's allocations. Other payments' allocations do not change.
- Payments are never deleted. Every approval, rejection, void and lease creation writes a row to audit_log (who, what, when, details).

### Allocation

When a payment becomes approved, its amount is allocated to the lease's invoices that still have something unpaid, in this order: due date, then deposit before rent, then period index. Each invoice is filled up to its unpaid amount before the next one, including invoices that are not due yet. Whatever is left once every invoice is fully paid is stored on the payment as unapplied_sen. Only online payments can end up with an unapplied amount, because manual payments are capped.
The paid amount of an invoice is the sum of its allocations. Statuses are computed with invoiceStatus, never stored.
All of this must stay correct when requests arrive at the same time. For example, two staff members recording payments on the same lease at once must not exceed the cap together, and a payment approved twice at once is allocated once.

### Collections report

The total of approved payments for each calendar month of received_at in Malaysia time, over a range of months, including months with nothing collected. With the seed data, Northwind's report for 2026-01 to 2026-03 is [{ month: '2026-01', collectedSen: 300000 }, { month: '2026-02', collectedSen: 0 }, { month: '2026-03', collectedSen: 200000 }].

## 5. Online Payments

A tenant pays online like this:

- The tenant clicks Pay now on their lease. Your API creates a gateway bill for the amount due now: the unpaid amounts of the lease's invoices due on or before today's Malaysia date. If nothing is due, refuse. Bill ids must be impossible to guess.
- In production the tenant would now be redirected to the gateway. In this test, show the bill id and amount: we play the gateway using the simulator below.
- The gateway calls your webhook, POST /api/webhooks/gateway. Only the webhook can settle a bill. The gateway also sends the tenant back to /payments/return?bill_id=...&paid=true. That page only shows the bill's real status from your database and changes nothing.

### Webhook

The request body is application/x-www-form-urlencoded, with these fields. The gateway may add more fields in future.
Field | Example | Notes |
id | bill_8f3a2c | Your bill id (this short example is guessable; yours must not be) |
paid | true | true or false |
paid_amount | 210050 | Amount in sen; 0 when not paid |
paid_at | 2026-04-01 00:30:12 +0800 | When it was paid |
transaction_id | TX-000123 | Gateway transaction id |
transaction_status | completed | completed, failed or pending |
x_signature | 06994f... | See below |

Signature. Take every field in the request except x_signature, sort them by key (ascending by character code), write each one as the key immediately followed by the value, join them with |, and compute the HMAC-SHA256 of the resulting string with your secret key GATEWAY_X_SIGNATURE_KEY, as lowercase hex. Test vector, with the key test_x_signature_key and the six example values above:
source: idbill_8f3a2c|paidtrue|paid_amount210050|paid_at2026-04-01 00:30:12 +0800|transaction_idTX-000123|transaction_statuscompleted
signature: 06994fab2d674e7829144eaa2204631716d3c099b503d38945e92b6296531641
Required behavior:
Situation | Response | Effect |
Signature missing or wrong | 401 | None |
Unknown bill id | 404 | None |
paid=true and paid_amount is not the bill's amount | 422 | None |
paid=true, bill pending or failed | 200 | Bill becomes paid, and one approved online payment is created with received_at = paid_at, then allocated |
paid=true, bill already paid (a repeat delivery) | 200 | None |
paid=false, bill pending | 200 | Bill becomes failed |
paid=false, bill already failed (a repeat delivery) | 200 | None |
paid=false, bill already paid (late or out of order) | 200 | None: a paid bill never goes back |

The gateway retries, so it may deliver the same callback several times, including at the same moment. A bill creates at most one payment, ever. Never log the secret key or whole callback payloads.

### Simulator

Save this as gateway-sim.mjs and run node gateway-sim.mjs <bill_id> <amount_sen> [true|false] with GATEWAY_X_SIGNATURE_KEY set.
import { createHmac } from 'node:crypto'

const [billId, amountSen, paid = 'true'] = process.argv.slice(2)
const url = process.env.WEBHOOK_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000/api/webhooks/gateway'
const key = process.env.GATEWAY_X_SIGNATURE_KEY

const myt = new Date(Date.now() + 8 _ 3600 _ 1000).toISOString()
const fields = {
id: billId,
paid,
paid_amount: paid === 'true' ? amountSen : '0',
paid_at: `${myt.slice(0, 10)} ${myt.slice(11, 19)} +0800`,
transaction_id: `TX-${Date.now()}`,
transaction_status: paid === 'true' ? 'completed' : 'failed',
}
const source = Object.keys(fields).sort().map(k => `${k}${fields[k]}`).join('|')
fields.x_signature = createHmac('sha256', key).update(source).digest('hex')

const res = await fetch(url, {
method: 'POST',
headers: { 'content-type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
body: new URLSearchParams(fields),
})
console.log(res.status, await res.text())

## 6. Access Control

Access is enforced in two places, and we test both:

- Your server code: route handlers, Server Actions and server components. Every endpoint must authenticate the caller and check their organization and role itself. A protected page or a hidden button is not a check.
- The Supabase Data API and Storage, which anyone holding your publishable key can call directly with their own access token.

### Server code

- Roles come from your memberships table, and from tenants.user_id for tenants. Never take a role or an organization from anything the user can edit, such as user_metadata.
- On the server, authenticate with supabase.auth.getUser() or getClaims(), not getSession().
- A request about a record in another organization, or another tenant's record, gets 404: do not reveal that it exists. A request about a record the caller can see, for an action their role does not allow, gets 403. A request without a valid login gets 401.
- IDs in request bodies are untrusted too. For example, a manager must not be able to create a lease on another organization's unit or tenant.
- Our tests call your API with Authorization: Bearer <access token>, where the token is a Supabase access token for one of the seeded users. Accept that header as well as the normal session cookie.
- The service role (secret) key must never reach the browser.

### Data API

This table is the most access allowed through the Supabase Data API, which is PostgREST called with a user's token. Granting less is fine where your app does not need it, with one exception: the tenant portal reads the tenant's own data, and updates their phone number, directly from the browser with supabase-js.
Table | anon | tenant | staff | manager |
organizations | none | read own organization | read own organization | read own organization |
memberships | none | none | read own organization | read own organization |
units | none | read the units of own leases | read own organization | read own organization |
tenants | none | read own row, update only phone | read own organization | read own organization |
leases, invoices, payments, payment_allocations, gateway_bills | none | read the rows of own leases | read own organization | read own organization |
audit_log | none | none | none | read own organization |

Every other insert, update or delete through the Data API must fail for everyone. This covers every table, view and function (/rest/v1/rpc/...) you create, not just the ones above. audit_log is append-only for every role, including the service role and the database owner.

### Storage

Bank transfer slips go in a private bucket named payment-slips, under <org_id>/.... Only staff and managers of that organization can upload there, and they read slips through short-lived signed URLs. Tenants, other organizations and anonymous users cannot read, list or upload slips. A payment's slip_path must point to an existing file in its own organization's folder.

## 7. HTTP API

Request and response bodies are JSON, except for the webhook. Amounts are integers in sen. Dates are YYYY-MM-DD, and instants are ISO 8601 with an offset. Errors return { "error": "message" }.
Method and path | Who | Success | Other responses |
POST /api/leases | manager | 201 { id } | 400 invalid input, 409 overlaps another lease on the unit |
GET /api/leases/:leaseId | staff, manager, the lease's tenant | 200, shape below | |
POST /api/leases/:leaseId/payments | staff, manager | 201 { id, status } | 400 invalid input, 422 over the cap |
POST /api/payments/:paymentId/approve | manager | 200 { status } | 409 not pending, 422 over the remaining balance |
POST /api/payments/:paymentId/reject | manager | 200 { status } | 400 missing reason, 409 not pending |
POST /api/payments/:paymentId/void | manager | 200 { status } | 400 missing reason, 409 not approved |
POST /api/leases/:leaseId/gateway-bills | the lease's tenant | 201 { billId, amountSen } | 422 nothing due |
GET /api/reports/collections?from=YYYY-MM&to=YYYY-MM | staff, manager | 200 [{ month: 'YYYY-MM', collectedSen }], one entry per month in order | 400 invalid range |
POST /api/webhooks/gateway | the gateway | see section 5 | |

Every endpoint also returns 401, 403 and 404 as described in section 6. Request bodies:
// POST /api/leases
{ unitId: string; tenantId: string; startDate: string; endDate: string; monthlyRentSen: number; depositSen: number }

// POST /api/leases/:leaseId/payments
{ amountSen: number; method: 'cash' | 'bank_transfer'; receivedAt: string; slipPath?: string }

// POST /api/payments/:paymentId/reject and POST /api/payments/:paymentId/void
{ reason: string }
GET /api/leases/:leaseId returns the invoices in allocation order:
{
lease: { id: string; unitId: string; tenantId: string; startDate: string; endDate: string; monthlyRentSen: number; depositSen: number }
invoices: {
id: string; kind: 'deposit' | 'rent'; periodIndex: number | null; periodStart: string | null; periodEnd: string | null
dueDate: string; amountSen: number; paidSen: number; status: InvoiceStatus
}[]
payments: {
id: string; amountSen: number; unappliedSen: number; method: 'cash' | 'bank_transfer' | 'online'
status: 'pending_verification' | 'approved' | 'rejected' | 'voided'; receivedAt: string
}[]
}
Creating a lease stores the lease and exactly the invoices generateSchedule returns, all or nothing. Leases on the same unit never overlap (both dates are inclusive), even when two requests arrive at the same moment.

## 8. Database

- Keep every database object in SQL migrations under supabase/migrations/: tables, constraints, RLS policies, grants, functions, triggers, and the storage bucket and its policies. npx supabase db reset must rebuild all of it; nothing may depend on changes made by hand in Supabase Studio. Use Prisma for server-side data access, with prisma/schema.prisma matching the database.
- Store money as integer sen (bigint), never as a floating-point type. Calendar dates are date, and instants are timestamptz.
- Required tables and columns (add whatever else you need):
  Table | Required columns |
  organizations | id, name |
  memberships | user_id, org_id, role (manager or staff) |
  units | id, org_id, name |
  tenants | id, org_id, user_id, full_name, email, phone |

One piece of work that acts on what this session just found stays here while this session has nothing else in flight ("Starting other sessions" says why): make it the box's question, with a button that has you do it here. A piece you left or could not verify is still this task, not a follow-up: finish or check it now, here or in a subagent, or name it in the recap. tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.

- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

schema.name: mcp__visualize__show_widget
schema.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.
